scope: New author inventory of fig-131 and fig-132 from original pixels only, before any modern draft. Each original opened once at original resolution; no crops, reopens, source pages, answer keys or previous modern figures.

observations: One shared spatial diagram, not separate panels. An upright, unlabelled plane patch containing triangle ABC overlaps a lower curved plane alpha.

The upright patch has an all-solid four-sided boundary: near-horizontal top through A, irregular descending left/right sides, near-horizontal bottom through C and B continuing to the right. A is on the top boundary, C and B on the bottom boundary; C is left of B.

A is above and slightly left of C. AC descends steeply right to C, AB descends diagonally right to B. AC and AB are solid throughout. C to B lies on the solid common horizontal boundary. Visible small black junction marks occur at A, C and B.

The lower alpha patch is a curved oval-like boundary. Its near/front/lower boundary is solid; its rear/upper boundary is dashed and rises behind the upright patch, crossing AC and AB in the projection. Alpha is labelled in the lower-left interior.

Line m passes through the common horizontal boundary strictly to the right of B; that intersection is unlabelled. Its lower-left/foreground part is solid; its upper-right/rear continuation is dashed. The line has no arrowhead. The m label is below/right of its foreground part.
A small projected right-angle marker lies immediately lower-left of the unlabelled intersection of m and the extended CB line. There is no right-angle marker at C.
The only source labels are A, C, B, m and alpha. There are no numeric givens, units, ticks, grids, vector arrows, lengths, equations or additional named points.

Edition givens: AC is perpendicular to alpha; AB is oblique; CB is its orthogonal projection. In the sufficiency proof m is in alpha and perpendicular to CB; the necessity argument exchanges the perpendicular premise. The source supports this published theorem/proof, not a new exercise answer.

observations: One alpha plane drawn as a closed irregular oval with an entirely solid boundary. No upright plane patch is drawn here. The alpha label is in its lower-left interior.

A lies above the plane, C below A at the perpendicular foot inside the left part of the oval, and B lies to the right of C inside the plane. There are no circular point dots at A, C or B; these labels name the vector junctions.

Three entirely solid directed vector shafts form the projected triangle: A to C downward with arrowhead at C, A to B diagonally down-right with arrowhead at B, C to B nearly horizontally right with arrowhead at B. They are not undirected segments.

A second solid line m runs from the lower/front boundary up-right to the rear/right boundary in the same plane. A visible dot M lies on this line in the lower-right interior. A directed arrow starts at M and ends at the upper-right endpoint N, whose label is to the right of the arrowhead. N has no circular dot.
The undirected solid carrier of m continues below M to the foreground plane boundary and beyond N to the rear plane boundary. The m label is left/below M.
The only labels are A, B, C, M, N, m and alpha. Every printed stroke is solid. There is no right-angle square, dashed stroke, numeric given, unit, equation, tick, coordinate axis or grid.

Task333 asks for a scalar-product proof of the three-perpendicular theorem. The image supplies the directions and coplanar carrier m, not the proof or a dot-product answer. It does not justify adding a right-angle mark to m or exposing equations.
